original_question: Is pseudocholinesterase deficiency an inherited condition that is caused by a dominant allele on an autosomal chromosome?

final_qi.question: Is pseudocholinesterase deficiency an inherited condition that is caused by a dominant allele on an autosomal chromosome?
final_qi.long_answer: Pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) deficiency is classically inherited as an autosomal-recessive trait, caused by loss-of-function mutations in the BCHE gene on chromosome 3. Individuals must carry two defective alleles to show the marked reduction in enzyme activity that leads to prolonged paralysis after succinylcholine or related agents; heterozygotes typically have only a mild or no clinical phenotype. Therefore, the condition is not produced by a dominant allele, but predominantly by recessive alleles on an autosomal chromosome.

0.question: Is pseudocholinesterase deficiency an inherited condition?

final_answer.long_answer: Pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) deficiency is classically inherited in an autosomal recessive (more precisely, codominant) manner. Pathogenic variants in both copies of the BCHE gene on chromosome 3 are usually required to produce the marked enzyme deficiency and the prolonged response to succinylcholine or other choline-ester drugs. Heterozygous carriers typically have intermediate enzyme activity but are not fully deficient. Therefore, it is not caused by a dominant allele; the inheritance pattern is autosomal recessive/codominant, not autosomal dominant.
